desc:
You may delete at most one element of nums (or delete nothing). After the deletion, the remaining elements close up into a shorter array. Return the largest possible length of a contiguous, strictly increasing run in the resulting array.

Example: nums = [1, 3, 5, 4, 7] returns 4: delete the 4 to get [1, 3, 5, 7]. Deleting the 5 instead gives [1, 3, 4, 7], also of length 4.
hints: Trying every deletion and rescanning costs O(n<sup>2</sup>). Which pieces of the original array get glued together by a deletion?
Deleting index i glues the strictly increasing run that ends at i - 1 to the strictly increasing run that starts at i + 1. The glue works only if nums[i - 1] < nums[i + 1].

Precompute endHere[i] (length of the increasing run ending at i) and startHere[i] (length of the run starting at i). The answer is the larger of the best plain run and endHere[i - 1] + startHere[i + 1] over all i with nums[i - 1] < nums[i + 1].
editorial: A deletion can only help by joining two runs that were separated by the deleted element. If we delete index i, the new run through the gap consists of the strictly increasing run ending at i - 1 followed by the strictly increasing run starting at i + 1; these two form one run exactly when nums[i - 1] < nums[i + 1]. The deleted element itself does not count towards the length.

Compute endHere with a left-to-right pass (endHere[i] = endHere[i - 1] + 1 if nums[i - 1] < nums[i], else 1) and startHere with a right-to-left pass. The answer is the maximum of the longest run in the untouched array (also the answer with no deletion) and endHere[i - 1] + startHere[i + 1] for each valid i from 1 to n - 2. Deleting the first or last element never creates a longer run than the plain maximum.
Three linear passes, O(n) time and O(n) space. The same idea of 'run ending here + run starting there' solves many 'at most one change' run problems.
